talk: Gross margin is how much of each dollar you keep after paying for the thing you sold. High margin gives you room for mistakes. Discounting attacks margin first, volume second.

terms.meaning: Price minus what the item cost you.
That margin as a share of the price.

questions.prompt: A home shirt costs $25 to make and sells for $70. What's the gross margin %?
whyNot: $25 / $70 = about 36% is the cost's share of the price. Margin is the part you keep.
$45 is the margin in dollars. As a share of the $70 price it's about 64%.
$70 is the price in dollars. It isn't a percentage of anything.

questions.prompt: End of season sale: shirts drop to $50. What's your margin per shirt now?
questions.hint: New price minus the same cost.
working: ($45 - $25) / $45 = about 44% off your margin. Discounts hit margin harder than price.
whyNot: $70 - $50 = $20 is how much the price fell, not what you keep.
$45 was the margin at full price. The cost stays $25 while the price drops.
$50 is the new price. You still pay $25 to make the shirt.

questions.prompt: You sold 1,000 shirts at full price. How many would you need to sell at $50 to make the same profit?
questions.hint: Full-price profit divided by sale margin.
working: (1,800 - 1,000) / 1,000 = 80% more shirts just to stand still.
whyNot: 1,000 x $25 = $25,000, well short of the $45,000 you made at full price.
2,500 x $25 = $62,500. That beats full price comfortably, so you need fewer.

takeaway: Discounts eat margin first. Know how much more you'd need to sell before you cut.
